title: Need One Bell-pair Only (NOBOL) for Low-Overhead Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
authors: Sean Grzenda, Shahram Babaie, Chunming Qiao
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation fundamentally relies on encoding a logical qubit into a structured block of physical qubits, typically in the tens to hundreds. As a trade-off for improved fault-tolerance, logical gate operations will incur a linear overhead in terms of both the amount of time and quantum resources than before. For example, in monolithic quantum computing, performing a gate operation on two distant logical qubits will first require using a linear number of SWAP operations in order to move the logical qubits next to each other; while in distributed quantum computing, doing so will first require a linear number of ancilla qubits in order to form entanglement connections (or a logical Bell pair).   In this paper, we focus on significantly reducing the overhead involved in logical CNOT operations, a fundamental primitive. We propose NOBOL, a novel approach that requires only one Bell pair to perform a logical CNOT operation on two distant qubits encoded in arbitrary CSS codes. More importantly, NOBOL only requires performing gate operations on the logical X or Z operator subsets of the logical qubits. For many CSS codes, such as the surface code, these subsets are significantly smaller than the size of the code itself. In this paper, we describe various circuit realizations of NOBOL, including a depth-optimal circuit with logarithmic depth in terms of the size of the logical operators. Finally, we propose effective methods to contain error propagation without incurring much additional overhead.   Since NOBOL can be effectively applied to a wide range of quantum error-correcting (QEC) codes and, in addition, is agnostic to qubit modalities and effective for various architectures, including those based on either a monolithic QPU or distributed QPUs.
summary: This paper introduces NOBOL, a protocol to perform logical CNOT gates between distant qubits using only one Bell pair, circumventing the high resource overhead associated with current fault-tolerant methods. By restricting operations to small logical operator subsets, NOBOL offers a scalable and code-agnostic solution for large-scale quantum computation architectures. This significantly advances the feasibility of distributed quantum networking.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is significantly reducing the overhead associated with performing logical CNOT operations between distant qubits in fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_result: The authors propose NOBOL, a novel protocol that achieves the logical CNOT using only a single pre-shared Bell pair, drastically reducing the resource overhead compared to previous linear or quadratic scaling methods.
method: The method leverages the fact that the operation can be restricted to acting only on the logical X or Z operator subsets of the qubits, which are assumed to be much smaller than the full code block size.
model_or_system: The work is situated in the context of fault-tolerant quantum computation using arbitrary CSS codes, applicable to both monolithic and distributed quantum processing units (QPUs).
key_observables: Logical CNOT operation success, resource overhead (number of Bell pairs/SWAP gates), and circuit depth.
important_parameters: The size of the logical operator subsets ($	au$), the code distance ($d$), and the physical link fidelity ($p_{	ext{link}}$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the logical CNOT can be realized by interacting only with the small subsets of physical qubits corresponding to the logical operators, and that error containment procedures can be effectively implemented.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the remote CNOT operation using a distributed Bell pair and show the evolution of surface code stabilizers during the CNOT circuit, distinguishing between different stabilizer types.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the high overhead of remote operations, introduces NOBOL as a solution requiring only one Bell pair, details the circuit realizations (including depth-optimal circuits), and concludes with effective methods for containing error propagation.
why_interesting: While focused on abstract quantum computation protocols, the resource management and error containment strategies discussed (e.g., stabilizing stabilizers) are highly relevant to designing physical quantum hardware architectures.
